title: Terraform apply hang & circuit-breaker playbook (private deployments)
content:
Purpose:
This playbook covers how to triage and recover from a Terraform apply that appears stuck or is progressing extremely slowly for private deployments (VPC/on-prem). It focuses on common causes we see at Redwood: remote-state/backend issues across VPC endpoints, provider plugin stalls, network egress/proxy hangups, and long-running cloud provider operations. Also includes a lightweight circuit-breaker and safe-rollback checklist to reduce blast radius during upgrades and module changes.

When to use this doc:
- Apply has been running >5 minutes with no resource progress logs.
- terraform shows repeated provider timeouts or stalls (provider plugin CPU at 0% on the host agent).
- Observed partial infrastructure created but apply never completes.

Quick summary (0–30s): immediate safety actions
- Pause: Do NOT run another terraform apply or destroy concurrently.
- Snapshot terminal output: save terraform output and any TF_LOG lines to a gist for later analysis.
- Mark incident channel and tag owners (owner + collaborators listed above).
- If using remote state with locks (DynamoDB/Consul/Cosmos/S3-lock), check lock table for a stale lock. DO NOT force-unlock until you confirm the apply is dead and no agent is actively writing.

First-pass triage (0–5 min)
1) Is Terraform still making API calls?
   - Check the terraform process on the runner: top/ps to see CPU and open fds.
   - If TF_LOG was enabled: scan logs for repeating RPCs or provider plugin stack traces.
2) Remote state & backend health (common for VPC/on-prem)
   - If S3-compatible remote state: curl the endpoint from the runner machine (curl -v -I https://s3-meti.private.company.local) and check TLS/MTU/proxy errors.
   - If using DynamoDB locks: aws dynamodb get-item --table-name tf-locks --key '{"LockID":{"S":"<workspace>"}}' --region <reg>  (or equivalent for non-AWS backends). Look for TTL/LastModified.
   - If Consul backend: consul operator raft list-peers / consul kv get lock/... ; check connectivity to consul server agents.
3) Network and DNS checks
   - dig +short remote-state-hostname; nslookup; check /etc/resolv.conf.
   - Check iptables/ebtables and host proxy env vars (HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY).
   - Validate MTU: ip link show && ping -M do -s 1400 <remote-state-ip> to detect fragmentation.
4) Provider plugin stall patterns
   - Look for long-running provider child processes (terraform-provider-aws, terraform-provider-kubernetes). If a plugin is stuck in a syscall (strace -p <pid>) you might see repeated connect()/read() syscalls.
   - Provider plugin cache corruption: check ~/.terraform.d/plugin-cache or the agent runner workspace. If corrupted, restart runner and clear plugin cache (with caution).

If apply has created resources but not completed (5–20 min)
- Check cloud provider consoles or on-prem orchestration UIs for in-progress operations (instances being created, IP allocation requests pending, storage attach). These external operations often block the provider until they finish.
- If the operation is stuck in the provider but the provider API shows in-progress for >10m, escalate to the cloud/infra owner to inspect the underlying operation.
- For Kubernetes resources: kubectl get events --all-namespaces | grep -i <resource> to see image-pull/backoff or admission webhook timeouts.

Safe force-unlock and abort pattern (only after confirmation)
1) Confirm no terraform agent is actively writing: lsof -p <pid> and network activity checks.
2) Backup remote state: terraform state pull > state.backup.json (store in secure location).
3) Force-unlock the workspace: terraform force-unlock -force <lock-id>.
4) If lock belonged to an automation runner (CI agent), look for that runner’s logs to ensure the run truly died.

Circuit-breaker for long/indeterminate applies (recommended pre-upgrade config)
- CI-runner timeout policy: default apply timeout = 30m for private deployments. After 20m with no resource events, runner should capture debug logs and mark the run as stalled but do not auto-unlock.
- Add a short-lived automation that creates a sentinel tag/annotation on long-running resources so operators can filter partial deployments.
- Keep an automated state snapshot schedule (daily) for private-workspaces used by Dedicated/Private customers to enable quick rollbacks.

Common root causes and focused probes
1) Backend/VPC endpoint policy denies S3/Dynamo calls from runner IPs
   - Symptoms: provider stalls with TLS handshake errors or 403s in TF_LOG.
   - Probe: curl against S3 endpoint from runner and from a control host outside the VPC to compare behavior.
2) Private CA/MTU/proxy rewriting TLS causing provider hangs
   - Symptoms: TLS handshake resets, repeated renegotiation, intermittent bytes transferred.
   - Probe: openssl s_client -connect <endpoint>:443 -showcerts ; tcpdump -n -s 0 -w /tmp/tf.pcap port 443 host <endpoint>.
3) Provider plugin mismatch / corrupted plugin binary
   - Symptoms: immediate SIGSEGV or plugin process exits then restarts; or hangs with zero CPU.
   - Probe: check terraform init logs, compare provider versions in .terraform.lock.hcl, run provider binary with --version if available.
4) Large resource graph + remote caching mismatches
   - Symptoms: apply stalls traversing many resources, slow refresh.
   - Probe: terraform plan -refresh=false to avoid refresh step; run apply with -parallelism=1 to surface failing resource.
5) On-prem artifact repositories (yum/apt/docker registry) unreachable
   - Symptoms: provisioners or post-install scripts waiting on package installs / image pulls.
   - Probe: from target host, curl registry endpoints and docker pull sample image; check imagePullSecrets.

Quick checklist to run in order (copyable)
- [ ] Save current terminal logs and TF_LOG output (if enabled).
- [ ] Check remote-state lock table (DynamoDB/Consul) and note LockID/CreatedAt.
- [ ] Run curl/openssl to remote-state endpoint from runner.
- [ ] Inspect terraform process CPU and open sockets (ps/top/lsof).
- [ ] Identify provider child processes and strace if safe.
- [ ] Check cloud/on-prem console for in-progress operations.
- [ ] Snapshot remote state: terraform state pull > state.backup.json.
- [ ] If safe, force-unlock then re-run plan to confirm state.
- [ ] If reapply needed, run with -parallelism=1 and TF_LOG=TRACE to capture failing resource.

Recommended commands and scripts (examples)
- Check lock (DynamoDB): aws dynamodb get-item --table-name tf-locks --key '{"LockID":{"S":"<workspace>"}}' --region us-west-2
- Force-unlock: terraform force-unlock -force <lock-id>
- Snapshot state: terraform state pull > /tmp/<workspace>-state-$(date +%s).json
- Provider debug run: TF_LOG=TRACE terraform apply -auto-approve -parallelism=1 > /tmp/tf-debug.log 2>&1 &
- Probe network connectivity: curl -vI --connect-timeout 8 https://<remote-state-hostname>/ || openssl s_client -connect <remote-state-hostname>:443 -brief

Rollback patterns (if apply created partial resources)
- Preferred: do a targeted terraform destroy for the affected module using -target= to remove partially created resources, then run a clean apply.
- If destroy fails due to provider API issues, coordinate with infra team to remove dangling resources via provider console/CLI, then import state back into terraform (terraform import ...) before reapplying.
- Avoid manual deletions without cleaning state unless you are prepared to run terraform state rm for those resources. Keep a saved copy of the pre-change state.

Post-incident checklist (for postmortem)
- Capture runner logs, remote-state backups, and cloud provider operation IDs.
- Record the trigger (PR / module / workspace), diff in .terraform.lock.hcl, and runner version.
- Update the module with clearer failure mode handling (timeouts, retryable errors).
- Consider adding a canary deployment stage for that module in the pipeline.

Minimal smoke-test checklist to run after recovery (run these from the same CI runner workspace)
- [ ] terraform init (succeeds, no new provider downloads unexpectedly)
- [ ] terraform plan -out=tfplan (plan computes quickly, no hanging refresh)
- [ ] apply the plan in a small test workspace with -parallelism=1 and a 10m runner timeout
- [ ] confirm remote-state lock is properly created and released
- [ ] verify created resources in cloud/on-prem manager (VMs up, IPs assigned, storage attached)
- [ ] for k8s: kubectl get pods -n <ns> and kubectl describe any CrashLoopBackOff
- [ ] smoke endpoint hit: curl -v http://<service-ip>:<port>/health (expect 200)

Notes and lessons we've learned
- Many private-deploy hangs are caused by subtle networking differences (proxy/MTU/endpoint policy). Always validate the runner’s network path to the remote-state backend as a priority.
- Agent restarts often surface a corrupted plugin binary; use a reproducible plugin-cache approach in CI to reduce drift.
- Conservative timeout policies and preflight checks (remote-state reachable, provider versions pinned) greatly reduce on-call load.

Appendix: quick reference commands
- List terraform child processes: ps aux | grep terraform | grep -v grep && pstree -p <parent-pid>
- Network capture for TLS issues: sudo tcpdump -w /tmp/tf-conn.pcap host <remote-state-ip> and share with security team.
- Restore state from backup: terraform state push /path/to/state.backup.json  (use with caution; prefer import/targeted destroy when possible).

If you hit an unfamiliar failure, ping #private-deployments and include: runner id, git ref, workspace name, state backup, and the commands you ran. Keep this doc updated with new patterns you observe.
